region.en: Ilocos coast, northwestern Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Ilocano tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋西北伊洛克斯海岸（伊洛卡諾故事圈之象徵定位）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Ilocano: 'The Monkey and the Turtle', eBook #12814

summary.en: The sad, hungry monkey joins the turtle in stealing banana plants, but plants his in a tree where it dies, while the turtle's rooted plant fruits. The monkey eats all the ripe fruit and is killed by the turtle's bamboo traps; the turtle cuts up the corpse, sells the meat to other monkeys, and when captured, tricks his captors into imitating his stone-weighted dive — the monkeys drown, and monkeys do not eat meat to this day.
summary.zh: 飢餓的猴子與海龜合夥偷香蕉苗；猴把苗種在樹上而枯死，龜的則結果纍纍。猴獨吞熟蕉，被龜以竹尖陷阱殺死；龜將猴屍切成肉塊賣給群猴，被擒時又誘群猴腰繫石頭潛水捕龍蝦——群猴溺斃，猴子至今不食肉。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Ilocano narrators; presented as an archival record. Classic trickster/counter-trickster animal cycle tale.

passages.text: A monkey, looking very sad and dejected, was walking along the bank of the river one day when he met a turtle. He was hungry, for the farmer's squash had all been taken by other monkeys, and the turtle told him not to be discouraged: take a bolo and follow him, and they would steal some banana plants. They dug up some nice plants, but the monkey climbed a tree and planted his in it, while the turtle, who could not climb, dug a hole in the ground and set his there. Weeks later the monkey's plant was dead, for its roots had had no soil in the tree, but the turtle's was tall and bearing fruit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Monkey and the Turtle'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The monkey sprang up the tree, leaving the poor turtle on the ground, and when the turtle begged for some to eat, the monkey threw him only a green one and ate all the ripe ones himself. When he had eaten all the good bananas the monkey stretched his arms around the tree and went to sleep. The turtle gathered sharp bamboo, stuck it all around under the tree, and cried, "Crocodile is coming! Crocodile is coming!" The monkey, startled, fell upon the sharp bamboo and was killed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Monkey and the Turtle'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The turtle cut the dead monkey into pieces, put salt on it, and dried it in the sun; the next day he sold the meat to other monkeys in the mountains for squash, calling back as he left: "Lazy fellows, you are now eating your own body." The monkeys ran and caught him. "Let us take a hatchet," said one, "and cut him into very small pieces" — but the turtle laughed, showing the black scars on his shell: "That is just what I like." "Let us throw him into the water," said another, and at this the turtle cried and begged for his life, so they threw him in. He soon came up with a lobster, and when the astonished monkeys begged to know how to catch lobsters, he said he had tied a stone to a string around his waist to sink. They all tied strings and stones and plunged into the water, never to come up again. And to this day monkeys do not like to eat meat, because they remember the ancient story.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Monkey and the Turtle'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Poor Fisherman and His Wife

region.en: Ilocos coast, northwestern Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Ilocano tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋西北伊洛克斯海岸（伊洛卡諾故事圈之象徵定位）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Ilocano: 'The Poor Fisherman and His Wife', eBook #12814

summary.en: A poor fisherman catches a great white fish he believes is the town priest; his wife thinks it is the governor. Terrified of discovery, they flee their village on a holiday, hear bells at Pilar and think the people are pursuing them, then rush home — where, mounting their sons' horse in panic and forgetting to untie its rope, the fruit that falls from the shaken caramay tree convinces them they are being shot, and they die of fright.
summary.zh: 貧漁夫網得大白魚，自以為網到鎮上神父，其妻則說是省長。二人懼罪逃亡，逢節日炮響鐘鳴，愈發驚恐；至皮拉爾聞鐘聲，以為追兵又至，折返回家。慌亂中夫婦騎上兒子繫於卡瑪伊樹的馬，忘了解繩；馬拉扯繩索震落滿樹果子，二人以為中彈，驚懼而亡。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Ilocano narrators; presented as an archival record. Comic fear-tale; taboo tag is interpretive (a forbidden catch treated as pollution and punished by panic).

passages.text: Many years ago a poor fisherman and his wife lived with their three sons in a village by the sea. One day the old man set his snare in the water, and at night found he had caught a great white fish such as he had never seen; it occurred to him that it was the priest of the town. He ran to his wife crying, "My wife, I have caught the priest!" But when she saw the fish she cried, "Oh, it is not the priest but the governor." The old man insisted it was the priest, and they went home trembling with fear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Poor Fisherman and His Wife'; not verbatim.

passages.text: That night neither slept for wondering what they should do. The next day was a great holiday: at four o'clock cannons were fired and bells rang loudly, and the old couple, hearing the noise and not knowing the reason, thought their crime had been discovered and the people were searching for them to punish them, so they fled to the woods. Reaching the woods near Pilar, they heard the sexton ringing the bells for mass and thought the people there had been notified of their escape, so they turned and started home again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Poor Fisherman and His Wife'; not verbatim.

passages.text: As they reached their house, the three sons tied their one horse to the trunk of the caramay tree, and at noon the bells rang again. Not thinking what time of day it was, the old man and woman ran out in terror, and seeing the horse, jumped on its back to ride to the next town before anyone could catch them — forgetting to untie the rope around the trunk. As they whipped the horse and it pulled at the rope, fruit fell from the tree upon the old man and woman. Believing they were shot, they were so frightened that they died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Poor Fisherman and His Wife'; not verbatim.

region.en: Ilocos coast, northwestern Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Ilocano tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋西北伊洛克斯海岸（伊洛卡諾故事圈之象徵定位）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Ilocano: 'The Presidente who had Horns', eBook #12814

summary.en: An unjust presidente wishes he had horns to frighten his people, and horns grow on his head. His barber, forbidden on pain of hanging to tell, digs a hole under the bamboo and whispers the secret into the ground — and the bamboo itself begins to say that the presidente has horns. The councilmen hear it, force their way in, and kill him, saying he was no better than an animal.
summary.zh: 暴虐的鎮長一怒之下想長角嚇人，角果真生出。理髮師奉命不得外洩（否則處死），回思難抑，掘穴於竹林之下，低聲道出秘密——竹子卻替他宣揚：鎮長長角了！議員聞之破門而入，見角而殺之，言其與獸無異。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Ilocano narrators; presented as an archival record. The whispered-secret motif (cf. Midas' barber) with the earth/bamboo broadcasting truth.

passages.text: Once there was a presidente who was very unjust to his people, and one day he became so angry that he wished he had horns so that he might frighten them. No sooner had he made this rash wish than horns began to grow on his head. He sent for a barber, and as the man worked the presidente asked what he saw on his head; the barber, though he could see the horns plainly, was afraid to say so. Soon the presidente felt the horns himself, and when he inquired again the barber told him he had two horns. "If you tell anyone what you have seen, you shall be hanged," said the presidente as the barber started away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Presidente who had Horns'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At home the barber did not intend to tell anyone, but as he thought of his secret the desire to tell became so strong that he knew he could not keep it. Finally he went to the field, dug a hole under some bamboo, crawled in, and whispered that the presidente had horns; then he filled up the hole and went home. By and by people passing the bamboo stopped in amazement, for a voice came from the trees saying that the presidente had horns. The news spread through the town and to the councilmen, who also heard the voice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Presidente who had Horns'; not verbatim.

passages.text: By this time the horns had grown a foot in length, and the presidente was so ashamed that he bade his wife say he could not talk. The councilmen insisted on seeing him, saying that if it were true he had horns he had no right to govern the people. She refused to let them in, so they broke down the door, saw the horns on the presidente's head, and killed him, saying he was no better than an animal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Presidente who had Horns'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Story of a Monkey: The Thorn That Cost a Tail
title.zh: 猴子的故事：一根刺換走一條尾

region.en: Ilocos coast, northwestern Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Ilocano tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋西北伊洛克斯海岸（伊洛卡諾故事圈之象徵定位）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Ilocano: 'The Story of a Monkey', eBook #12814

summary.en: A monkey with a thorn in his tail pays the barber with his tail-tip for the razor that cuts it off, then exacts the old woodcutter's firewood for his broken razor, the cake-maker's cakes for his burned wood, and dies just as he prospers — bitten by a dog which eats all the cakes.
summary.zh: 猴尾入刺，以尾梢換得理髮師的剃刀；又以斷刀換得老嫗的柴，以燒盡的柴換得婦人的糕餅。得逞之際卻被狗咬死，狗食盡其糕餅。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Ilocano narrators; presented as an archival record. Cumulative chain-bargain trickster tale ending in the trickster's own death.

passages.text: One day when a monkey was climbing a tree in the forest he ran a thorn into his tail, and try as he would he could not get it out. He went to a barber in the town and offered to pay well to have it pulled; the barber tried with his razor, but in doing so cut off the end of the tail. The monkey cried, "Barber, Barber, give me back my tail, or give me your razor!" and as the barber could not put the tail back, he gave him the razor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Story of a Monkey'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the way home the monkey met an old woman cutting wood, and lent her the razor to cut more easily; before long it broke, and the monkey demanded a new one or all the firewood. She could not get a new razor, so she gave him the firewood. Going back to town to sell it, he saw a woman making cakes beside the road, and gave her his wood to bake more cakes; when the last stick was burned he cried that she must give him all her cakes, and she did. The monkey took the cakes and started for the town, but on the way he met a dog which bit him so that he died, and the dog ate all the cakes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Story of a Monkey'; not verbatim.

region.en: Ilocos coast, northwestern Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Ilocano tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋西北伊洛克斯海岸（伊洛卡諾故事圈之象徵定位）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Ilocano: 'The White Squash', eBook #12814

summary.en: A childless old couple whose garden always bore finds the vines suddenly barren; after long waiting one white squash grows. Opening it, they hear a voice begging them to be careful — inside is a talking baby boy. His bath water turns to gold, but on the third morning the child grows sad, flies away, and all the gold disappears, leaving the couple poor and alone again.
summary.zh: 無子的老夫婦花園常年結果，某年藤蔓忽然不結；久待之後僅得一白南瓜。剖瓜時瓜內傳聲請求小心——裡面竟是會說話的男嬰。嬰兒沐浴之水滴落皆化黃金；第三日晨，孩兒憂傷地飛去，黃金同時消失，老夫婦復歸於貧獨。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Ilocano narrators; presented as an archival record. Miraculous birth from a plant; the vanishing-guest ending.

passages.text: In a queer little bamboo house in front of a big garden lived a man and his wife all alone. They had always been kind and good to everyone, but they were not happy, because the child for which they longed had never come, though they had prayed for a son or daughter every day for many years. In their garden grew fine white squash, and the vines bore the year around so they had never been in need of food — until one day they discovered that no new squash had formed to take the place of those they had picked.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The White Squash'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Each day they examined the vines; the big yellow flowers bloomed and faded, but no squash grew on the stems. Finally one morning the woman cried out with delight, for she had discovered a little green squash. They decided to let it ripen for seed, and eagerly watched it grow into a beautiful white vegetable; but by the time it was large enough for food they were so hungry that they decided to eat it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The White Squash'; not verbatim.

passages.text: They brought a large knife and picked it, but scarcely had they started to open it when a voice cried out from within, "Please be careful that you do not hurt me." Thinking a spirit had spoken, they stopped; but when the voice again begged them to open the squash, they carefully opened it, and there inside was a nice baby boy who could already stand alone and talk. The couple were overjoyed. When the woman bathed him, the drops of water falling from his body were immediately changed to gold, until gold pieces covered the mat; a second bath brought more gold, enough to build a large house. But the third morning, when she brought the water, the boy grew very sad and flew away, and at the same time all the gold disappeared, and the man and his wife were left poor and alone.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The White Squash'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Story of Benito: The Servant Who Outdid the King
title.zh: 貝尼托的故事：僕從勝於王

region.en: Laguna lake region, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Tagalog tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋拉古納湖區（他加祿故事圈之象徵定位）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Tagalog: 'The Story of Benito', eBook #12814

summary.en: Poor Benito enters a king's service and is sent to free a princess kept by giants across the sea. A bound sparrow-hawk, the King of the Fishes, and a magic sword from a strange woman help him. The princess then sets the king three impossible tasks — a lost ring, a lost earring, water from heaven and the lower world — which Benito fulfills with the fish-king, the mouse-king, and the dying sparrow-hawk; when the king bathes in the lower-world water and becomes a monster, the princess marries Benito, who becomes king.
summary.zh: 貧童貝尼托入宮為僕，受命渡海營救被巨人看守的公主。獲雀鷹、魚王相助，並得神劍誅巨人。公主卻向國王連出三難題：海底之戒指、林中耳環、天上與下界之水——皆由貝尼托借魚王、鼠王、雀鷹之力完成。國王以下界之水沐浴，化為怪物；公主遂嫁忠僕貝尼托，夫婦共治王國。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Tagalog narrators; presented as an archival record. Tale-type: the prince's tasks fulfilled by the faithful servant.

passages.text: Benito was an only son who lived with his father and mother in a little village; they were very poor, and as the boy grew older he dreamed of being a help to them. Hearing of a young king who lived in a beautiful palace some distance away, he persuaded his parents to let him go and ask for work, and at last secured a place as a servant. One day the king sent for him: "I want you to bring to me a beautiful princess who lives in a land across the sea. Go at once, and if you fail you shall be punished severely." Benito's heart sank, but he answered, "I will, my lord."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Story of Benito'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In a thick forest he freed a large bird bound tightly with strings, which promised to help him whenever he called, its name being Sparrow-hawk. At the sea the King of the Fishes carried him on his back to the farther shore, and a strange woman gave him a magic sword that would kill instantly whatever it touched. At the castle many unarmed giants ran out to seize him, but he touched those in front with the sword and they fell dead, the others fleeing in panic. Benito freed the princess, who gladly returned with him to the palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Story of Benito'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the king asked the princess to be his wife, she demanded first the ring she had lost crossing the sea. Benito's friend the King of the Fishes summoned all his subjects, found one fish too full to swim hiding under a stone, and had it cut open — inside was the lost ring. The princess next demanded the earring she lost in the forest: the King of Mice summoned his subjects and found one little mouse too full to walk in a hole among the bamboo; cut open, it yielded the earring. The princess's last request was some water from heaven and some from the lower world, and the king sent Benito on the hardest errand of all.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Story of Benito'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Benito called Sparrowhawk, who consented to fetch the water; two light cups of bamboo were fastened to the bird's legs, and it returned at nightfall with water from heaven on its right foot and from the lower world on its left. The journey had been too much for the bird and it was dying, and Benito sorrowfully buried it before hastening to the palace. The princess had herself cut in two and the water of heaven poured over her, growing into the most beautiful woman the king had ever seen. Eager to be handsome, the king begged the water of the lower world for himself: cut and bathed, he became a creature most ugly and horrible, which soon vanished out of sight. The princess then chose Benito, so faithful to his master and so kind to her, for her husband; they were married amid great festivities and became king and queen of that broad and fertile land, and Benito never forgot his parents, giving them one of the finest portions of his kingdom.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Story of Benito'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Adventures of Juan: The Goat, the Net, the Pot, and the Beating Stick
title.zh: 胡安歷險記：羊、網、飯鍋與神棍

region.en: Laguna lake region, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Tagalog tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋拉古納湖區（他加祿故事圈之象徵定位）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Tagalog: 'The Adventures of Juan', eBook #12814

summary.en: Lazy Juan spares a magic tree in exchange for a goat that shakes silver from its whiskers, a fish-filled net, and a self-replenishing pot — each of which his tuba-drinking friend steals and replaces with a common one, earning Juan beatings from his family. The fourth gift, a stick that beats anything at the words "Boombye, Boomba," defeats the thief and recovers all the treasures; Juan beats his scolding family until they make him head of the house, kills robbers, and marries a princess.
summary.zh: 懶惰的胡安饒過一棵魔樹，換得鬚間落銀之羊、自滿魚網與永不空乏的飯鍋——但每次都在朋友灌醉後被換成凡品，回家還挨打。第四次他得一根說「Boombye, Boomba」便自動打人的神棍，制服竊賊，取回全部寶物；又教訓譏其一生之家人，令其尊他為家主；後以神棍退賊、娶得公主。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Tagalog narrators; presented as an archival record. The Juan cycle — the trickster hero whose luck and literal-mindedness carry the day.

passages.text: Juan was always getting into trouble: a lazy boy without good sense, whose family scolded and beat him whenever he did anything wrong. His mother gave him a bolo and sent him to the forest to cut firewood. Juan walked leisurely along, contemplating means of escape, until he came to a tree that seemed easy to cut — but it was a magic tree, and it said to him, "If you do not cut me I will give you a goat that shakes silver from its whiskers." Pleased both by curiosity and by not having to chop wood, Juan agreed at once, the bark separated, and a goat stepped out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Adventures of Juan'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the way home he met a friend more cunning than himself, who, knowing Juan's fondness for tuba, persuaded him to drink and substituted a common goat for the magic one while he was drunk. At home, when Juan commanded the animal to shake its whiskers, no money fell out, and his family, believing it another of Juan's tricks, beat and scolded him. He went back and threatened to cut the tree down for lying, but it offered a net which, cast on dry ground or even in the treetops, would return full of fish; the same friend again got him drunk and replaced the net with a common one, and again Juan was ridiculed at home. A third time the tree offered a magic pot, always full of rice, with spoons that provided whatever he wished to eat with it — and a third time the friend's tuba and substitution made Juan the subject of harder beatings.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Adventures of Juan'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Thoroughly angered, Juan sought the tree a fourth time and was on the point of cutting it down when it offered a stick which, at the words "Boombye, Boomba," would beat and kill anything he wished. When the friend asked what he had, Juan said, "Oh, it is only a stick, but if I say 'Boombye, Boomba' it will beat you to death." At the sound of the magic words the stick leaped from his hands and beat the friend until he cried that he would give back everything he had stolen. Juan then compelled the man to lead the goat and carry the net, jar, and spoons to his home; the goat shook its whiskers until his mother and brothers had all the silver they could carry, and they ate from the magic jar until filled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Adventures of Juan'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Juan said to his family, "You have beaten me and scolded me all my life, and now you are glad to accept my good things. I am going to show you something else: 'Boombye, Boomba'." The stick leaped out and beat them all until they begged for mercy and promised that Juan should ever after be head of the house. From that time Juan was rich and powerful, never going anywhere without his stick; one night when thieves came to his house he would have been robbed and killed had not the magic words caused the death of all the robbers. Some time after this he married a beautiful princess, and because of the kindness of the magic tree they always lived happily.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Adventures of Juan'; not verbatim.

region.en: Laguna lake region, Luzon, Philippines (symbolic pin for the Tagalog tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋拉古納湖區（他加祿故事圈之象徵定位）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Tagalog: 'Juan Gathers Guavas', eBook #12814

summary.en: Sent for ripe guavas to feed his father's guests, Juan eats all he can hold, then plays a joke instead of a feast: he bags a wasp's nest, locks the guests in, and watches. When his father opens the basket the wasps swarm the locked room, and the guests fight to escape through the windows — Juan opens the door and cries, "What fine, rich guavas you must have had! They have made you all so fat!"
summary.zh: 父親命胡安摘熟番石榴招待客人；胡安吃飽後卻以玩笑代盛宴——將黃蜂窩裝籃送入，反鎖房門。父親開籃，黃蜂滿室亂飛，賓客奪窗而逃。胡安開門見眾人臉腫，喊道：「你們吃的番石榴多麼肥美！把大家都吃胖了！」

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Tagalog narrators; presented as an archival record. Short Juan-cycle trickster anecdote.

passages.text: One day Juan's father sent him to get some ripe guavas, for a number of the neighbors had come in and he wanted to give them something to eat. Juan went to the guava bushes and ate all the fruit he could hold, and then he decided to play a joke on his father's guests instead of giving them a feast of guavas. A wasp's nest hung near by, and with some difficulty he succeeded in taking it down and putting it into the tight basket he had brought for the fruit.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Juan Gathers Guavas'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He hastened home and gave the basket to his father, and as he left the room where the guests were seated he closed the door and fastened it. As soon as Juan's father opened the basket the wasps flew over the room, and when the people found the door locked they fought to get out of the windows. After a while Juan opened the door, and when he saw the swollen faces of the people he cried, "What fine, rich guavas you must have had! They have made you all so fat!"
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Juan Gathers Guavas'; not verbatim.

region.en: Cebu-Bohol seas, central Philippines (symbolic pin for the Visayan tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓中部宿霧薄荷海域（米沙鄢故事圈之象徵定位）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Visayan: 'The Sun and the Moon', eBook #12814

summary.en: The Sun and Moon were married with many star children, but the Sun's burning embrace destroyed the children he tried to hug, and the Moon forbade him to touch them. While she was washing at the spring he disobeyed and several children perished; in fury she raised a banana tree to strike him, and he threw sand in her face — the dark marks still on the Moon's face — and has chased her ever since, sometimes almost catching her.
summary.zh: 日月成婚，育有眾星辰子女；太陽欲擁抱子女，卻灼熱傷之，月亮遂禁其靠近。月亮去泉邊浣衣時，太陽違禁害死數子；月怒舉蕉樹擊之，太陽揚沙迷其面——月面暗痕至今可見——並自此永世追逐月亮，時近時遠。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Visayan narrators; presented as an archival record. Celestial-family myth explaining moon markings and the sun's pursuit.

passages.text: Once upon a time the Sun and the Moon were married, and they had many children who were the stars. The Sun was very fond of his children, but whenever he tried to embrace any of them, he was so hot that he burned them up. This made the Moon so angry that finally she forbade him to touch them again, and he was greatly grieved.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Visayan 'The Sun and the Moon'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day the Moon went down to the spring to do some washing, and when she left she told the Sun that he must not touch any of their children in her absence. When she returned, however, she found that he had disobeyed her, and several of the children had perished. She was very angry, and picked up a banana tree to strike him, whereupon he threw sand in her face, and to this day you can see the dark marks on the face of the Moon. Then the Sun started to chase her, and they have been going ever since: sometimes he gets so near that he almost catches her, but she escapes, and by and by she is far ahead again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Visayan 'The Sun and the Moon'; not verbatim.

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Visayan: 'The First Monkey', eBook #12814

summary.en: A lazy grandson who gambles daily throws coconut shells at his industrious grandmother, who whips him with her cotton spindle — and he is transformed into an ugly animal, the cotton becoming his body hair and the stick his tail. He runs down to the town and whips his fellow gamblers with his tail, turning them into animals like himself; the people drive them all out, and they have lived in the trees as monkeys ever since.
summary.zh: 懶惰好賭的孫子因晚飯未備而擲椰殼擊打勤勞的祖母；祖母以紡錘抽打，少年頓化醜獸——棉花成其毛，紡錘成其尾。他奔下山，以尾抽打賭友，使之盡化同類。鎮民將他們逐出，從此棲於樹上，是為猴子。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Visayan narrators; presented as an archival record. Etiological transformation tale.

passages.text: Many years ago at the foot of a forest-covered hill was a small town, and just above it on the hillside was a little house in which lived an old woman and her grandson. The old woman, very industrious, earned their living by removing the seeds from cotton, keeping near at hand a basket of cotton and a long stick she used for a spindle. The boy was lazy and would do nothing to help his grandmother, but went down to the town every day to gamble.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The First Monkey'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day, when he had been losing money, the boy went home and was cross because his supper was not ready. "I am hurrying to get the seeds out of this cotton," said the grandmother, "and as soon as I sell it, I will buy us some food." At this the boy fell into a rage and picked up some cocoanut shells and threw them at his grandmother. She became angry and began to whip him with her spindle, when suddenly he was changed into an ugly animal, the cotton becoming hair which covered his body, while the stick itself became his tail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The First Monkey'; not verbatim.

passages.text: As soon as the boy found he had become an ugly creature he ran down into the town and began whipping his companions, the gamblers, with his tail, and immediately they were turned into animals like himself. The people would no longer have them in the town, but drove them out; they went to the forest where they lived in the trees, and ever since they have been known as monkeys.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The First Monkey'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Virtue of the Cocoanut: The Hunter and the Tuba

region.en: Cebu-Bohol seas, central Philippines (symbolic pin for the Visayan tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓中部宿霧薄荷海域（米沙鄢故事圈之象徵定位）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Visayan: 'The Virtue of the Cocoanut', eBook #12814

summary.en: A hunter finds the first cocoanut tree and digs it up to take home; when the leaves wilt, he revives it in turn with the blood of the noisy bird, the mocking monkey, and the wild pig his dog has helped him kill. Planted at home it grows into a tall tree — the first from which tuba was drawn. The hunter teaches that the tree is like the three animals: the drinker of a few cups grows noisy as the bird, more makes him silly as the monkey, and the drunk sleeps like the pig in the mud-hole.
summary.zh: 獵人發現第一株椰樹，掘起帶回；葉屢枯，他依次以鳥、猴、豬之血澆灌使之復甦。植於家中成巨樹——第一株取椰酒之樹。獵人以此訓誡：飲椰酒三、四杯者聒噪如鳥，多飲者愚癲如猴，爛醉者則如泥塘酣睡之豬。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Visayan narrators; presented as an archival record. Etiology of tuba and a temperance parable.

passages.text: One day a man took his blow-gun and his dog and went to the forest to hunt. Making his way through the thick woods, he chanced upon a young cocoanut tree growing in the ground, the first tree of this kind he had ever seen, and it seemed so peculiar that he stopped to look at it. Farther on he shot a noisy bird with his blow-gun, took aim at a large monkey that mocked him from a treetop, and that too fell dead at his feet; then, hearing his dog barking furiously, he hastened to it and found it biting a wild pig, which he killed after a hard struggle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Virtue of the Cocoanut'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Satisfied with his success, the hunter took the three animals on his back and returned to the little plant. "I have decided to take you home with me, little plant," he said, "for I like you and you may be of some use to me." He dug it up carefully, but before he had gone far the leaves began to wilt, and having no water, he in despair cut the throat of the bird and sprinkled the blood on the cocoanut; the plant revived. When the leaves wilted again he revived it with the blood of the monkey, and a third time with the blood of the pig.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Virtue of the Cocoanut'; not verbatim.

passages.text: This was his last animal, so he made all the haste possible to reach home before his plant died. The cocoanut wilted again before he reached his house, but when he planted it in the ground it quickly revived and grew into a tall tree. This hunter was the first man to take the liquor called tuba from the cocoanut tree, and he told his friends: "The cocoanut tree is like the three animals whose blood gave it life when it would have died. The man who drinks three or four cups of tuba becomes like the noisy bird that I shot with my blow-gun. One who drinks more than three or four cups becomes like the big monkey that acts silly; and one who becomes drunk is like the pig that sleeps even in a mud-hole."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Virtue of the Cocoanut'; not verbatim.

title.en: Mansumandig, the Man Who Leans Back and Thinks

region.en: Cebu-Bohol seas, central Philippines (symbolic pin for the Visayan tale cycle)
region.zh: 菲律賓中部宿霧薄荷海域（米沙鄢故事圈之象徵定位）

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Visayan: 'Mansumandig', eBook #12814

summary.en: To help his poor household, Mansumandig carries rice to the mines daily — but sells it for exactly the twenty-five centavos he paid, all year. Balancing accounts, he has made nothing; ashamed, he leans his head against the wall and thinks, which is why he is called Mansumandig. His wife then takes the same capital, weaves hemp into cloth, and makes three hundred pesos in a year; pitying him, she gives him the money to buy ten carabao, and they live comfortably ever after.
summary.zh: 曼蘇曼迪為養家而做米糧生意，卻整年以原價二十五分錢賣出。年底結帳分文未賺，羞愧地靠牆沉思——「曼蘇曼迪」（靠牆想者）之名由此而來。妻子以同樣本錢織麻布，一年掙得三百比索；她憐夫而以錢購十頭水牛耕田，從此生活安適。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Visayan narrators; presented as an archival record. Humorous teaching tale on wit and industry; also etiological for the saying about leaning back and thinking.

passages.text: One day a man said to his wife: "My wife, we are getting very poor and I must go into business to earn some money." With his twenty-five centavos he bought a half-cavan of rice and carried it on his shoulder to the mines, where the people eagerly bought it — for the regular price of twenty-five centavos. His wife rejoiced that they would become very rich, and the man went on with his business for a year, each day buying a half-cavan of rice and selling it for the price he had paid for it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Mansumandig'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then one day his wife said they would balance accounts, and she spread a mat on the floor. When she asked for the money he had made during the year, he handed her the twenty-five centavos. "Is that all you have received this year?" she cried angrily. He had paid twenty-five centavos and received twenty-five centavos. "Oh, my husband, how can you make any gain if you sell it for just what you paid for it?" The man leaned his head against the wall and thought; ever since then he has been called "Mansumandig," a man who leans back and thinks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Mansumandig'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the wife took the twenty-five centavos, bought hemp at the field where the people were gathering it, and wove it into cloth night and day — eight varas, sold for twelve and a half centavos a vara, the money reinvested in more hemp. At the end of a year she poured out her blanket of money, held aside her capital of twenty-five centavos, and counted three hundred pesos. Mansumandig, greatly ashamed that he had not made a cent, leaned his head against the wall and thought. After a while the woman pitied him, gave him the money, and told him to buy carabao; he bought ten and plowed his fields, and by raising good crops they lived comfortably all the rest of their lives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Mansumandig'; not verbatim.

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Visayan: 'Why Dogs Wag their Tails', eBook #12814

summary.en: A rich man sends his dog and cat to carry a magic ring to his daughter at a convent. The dog bullies the cat into giving up the ring at the river crossing, drops it in the swift water, and flees in fear before reaching home. The cat returns alone to face the master, who commands all dogs in the world to join the search and have their tails cut off if found guilty — which is why every dog that meets another shows his teeth and wags his tail to prove his innocence, and why cats fear water.
summary.zh: 富人遣犬貓護送魔戒至修道院的女兒處。渡河時犬強奪魔戒，卻失手落入急流，未及回家便畏罪而逃。貓獨自回去面對主人；主人下令天下之犬搜捕此犬，見者截其尾——是以犬犬相遇必亮齒搖尾以自清白；貓亦自始懼水。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Visayan narrators; presented as an archival record. Etiological animal tale.

passages.text: A rich man in a certain town once owned a dog and a cat, both very useful to him: the dog was old and toothless but a good guide, the cat strong and cunning. His daughter attended school at a convent some distance away, and very often he sent the two animals with presents. One day he called the faithful animals and bade them carry a magic ring to his daughter, the cat to carry it and the dog to guide her and keep her from harm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Why Dogs Wag their Tails'; not verbatim.

passages.text: All went well until they came to a river with neither bridge nor boat. As they were about to plunge into the water the dog said, "Let me take the magic ring." The cat refused — the master had given it to her to carry — but the dog argued that she could not swim well and threatened to kill her, and she reluctantly gave it up. The river was wide and the water swift, and just before they reached the opposite bank the dog dropped the ring. They searched carefully but could not find it anywhere; and just before reaching the house to report the loss, the dog was so overcome with fear that he turned and ran away and was never seen again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Why Dogs Wag their Tails'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The cat went on alone, and when the master saw her coming he called out to know what had become of her companion. The frightened cat explained how the ring had been lost and how the dog had run away. The master was very angry, and commanded that all his people should search for the dog, and that it should be punished by having its tail cut off. He also ordered that all the dogs in the world should join in the search — and ever since, when one dog meets another he says, "Are you the old dog that lost the magic ring? If so, your tail must be cut off." Then immediately each shows his teeth and wags his tail to prove that he is not the guilty one. Since then, too, cats have been afraid of water and will not swim across a river if they can avoid it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'Why Dogs Wag their Tails'; not verbatim.

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Visayan: 'The Hawk and the Hen', eBook #12814

summary.en: A hawk wins a hen's promise to marry him once she has grown wings like his, giving her a ring as an engagement present. The cock claims her as his own and makes her throw the ring away. When the hawk returns with her dress of feathers, the frightened hen lies that a snake made her lose it; knowing she deceives him, the hawk decrees that she must always scratch the ground to look for the ring, and every chicken he finds he will snatch away — which hens do to this day.
summary.zh: 鷹向母雞求婚，雞允諾待其翅膀長成如鷹時成婚；鷹以戒指為聘。公雞卻聲稱雞本屬於他，逼其棄戒。鷹攜美羽而至，見戒已失；母雞謊稱蛇嚇致失。鷹洞穿其謊，判罰：母雞必須終生抓地覓戒，且其雛雞凡被鷹見者必遭奪取——母雞抓地之習至今猶然。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Visayan narrators; presented as an archival record. Etiological animal tale of broken promise and punishment.

passages.text: A hawk flying about in the sky one day decided that he would like to marry a hen whom he often saw on earth. He flew down and searched until he found her, and then asked her to become his wife. She at once gave her consent on the condition that he would wait until she could grow wings like his, so that she might also fly high. The hawk agreed to this and flew away, after giving her a ring as an engagement present and telling her to take good care of it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Hawk and the Hen'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The hen was very proud of the ring and placed it around her neck. The next day, however, she met the cock, who looked at her in astonishment and said, "Where did you get that ring? Do you not know that you promised to be my wife? You must not wear the ring of anyone else. Throw it away." And the hen threw away the beautiful ring.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Hawk and the Hen'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Not long after, the hawk came down bringing beautiful feathers to dress the hen. Frightened, she hid behind the door, but came out when he called — and the hawk at once saw that the ring was gone. The hen, ashamed to tell the truth, answered that a large snake had frightened her so in the garden that she ran to the house and then missed the ring. The hawk looked sharply at her, knowing she was deceiving him, and said: "When you have found the ring I will come down again and make you my wife. But as a punishment for breaking your promise, you must always scratch the ground to look for the ring. And every chicken of yours that I find, I shall snatch away." Then he flew away, and ever since all the hens throughout the world have been scratching to find the hawk's ring.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Hawk and the Hen'; not verbatim.

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Visayan: 'The Spider and the Fly', eBook #12814

summary.en: Mr. Spider courts Miss Fly many times and is refused; when she closes her doors and windows against him and throws boiling water at his call, he vows everlasting enmity for himself and his descendants — which is why the spider still hates the fly to this day.
summary.zh: 蜘蛛先生屢次向蒼蠅小姐求婚均遭拒；一日她閉門閉窗，以滾水潑之。蜘蛛怒誓：己身及其子孫永世仇視蒼蠅、不得安寧——蜘蛛與蒼蠅之仇恨至今猶存。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Visayan narrators; presented as an archival record. Short etiological tale; taboo tag interpretive (a hostile act answered with an enduring curse).

passages.text: Mr. Spider wanted to marry Miss Fly. Many times he told her of his love and begged her to become his wife, but she always refused, for she did not like him. One day when she saw Mr. Spider coming again, Miss Fly closed all the doors and windows of her house and made ready a pot of boiling water. When Mr. Spider called, begging her to allow him to enter, she answered by throwing boiling water at him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Spider and the Fly'; not verbatim.

passages.text: This made Mr. Spider very angry, and he cried: "I will never forgive you for this, but I and my descendants will always despise you. We will never give you any peace." Mr. Spider kept his word, and even today one can see the hatred of the spider for the fly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Spider and the Fly'; not verbatim.

source.work: Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), Christianized Tribes, Visayan: 'The Battle of the Crabs', eBook #12814

summary.en: The land crabs hold a council and decide to make war on the waves that sing so loudly they cannot sleep. A shrimp mocks their weak legs, is pinched into promising help, then laughs at and flees the first wave — while the crabs, all looking toward the shore, are covered with water and drowned.
summary.zh: 陸蟹集會，決議向終夜喧唱、令其不得安眠的海浪宣戰。蝦譏其腿弱，被鉗迫允諾助戰，旋即見浪而逃；眾蟹皆望岸而立，為浪所覆，盡數溺斃。

sensitivity.note: Philippine oral tradition recorded from Visayan narrators; presented as an archival record. Short comic etiological tale.

passages.text: One day the land crabs had a meeting, and one of them said, "What shall we do with the waves? They sing so loudly all the time that we cannot possibly sleep." "Well," answered one of the oldest of the crabs, "I think we should make war on them." The others agreed, and it was decided that the next day all the male crabs should get ready to fight the waves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Battle of the Crabs'; not verbatim.

passages.text: As they started for the sea they met a shrimp, who asked where they were going. "We are going to fight the waves," answered the crabs, "for they make so much noise at night that we cannot sleep." "I do not think you will succeed," said the shrimp, "for the waves are very strong and your legs are so weak that even your bodies bend almost to the ground when you walk" — and he laughed loudly. This made the crabs very angry, and they pinched the shrimp until he promised to help them win the battle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Battle of the Crabs'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then they all went to the shore. But the crabs noticed that the eyes of the shrimp were set unlike their own, so they thought his must be wrong and laughed at him: "Friend shrimp, your face is turned the wrong way. What weapon have you to fight with the waves?" "My weapon is a spear on my head," replied the shrimp — and just then he saw a big wave coming and ran away. The crabs did not see it, however, for they were all looking toward the shore, and they were covered with water and drowned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Mabel Cook Cole, Philippine Folk Tales (1916), 'The Battle of the Crabs'; not verbatim.
